blocks.text: I
In Praise of the Lord
A is the starting-point of the world of sound: even so is the Great Original the starting-point of all that exists.
Of what avail is all thy learning if thou worship not the holy feet of Him of the perfect intelligence?
Whoso taketh refuge in the sacred feet of Him whose walk is among flowers, his days will be many upon the earth.
Behold the men who cleave unto the feet of Him who is beyond preference and beyond aversion: the ills of life touch them not ever.
Behold the men who sing earnestly the praises of the Lord: they will be freed from the pain-engendering fruits of action both good and evil.3
Behold the men who follow the righteous ways of Him who hath burned away the desires of the five senses: their days will be many upon the earth.
They alone escape from sorrow who take refuge in the feet of Him who hath no equal.
The stormy seas of wealth and sense delights cannot be traversed except by those who cling to the feet of the Sage who is the Ocean of Righteousness.
Worthless indeed like the organs of sense which do not perceive is the head that boweth not at the feet of Him who is endowed with the eight attributes.4
They alone cross the ocean of births and deaths who take refuge in the feet of the Lord: the others traverse it not.
II
In Praise of Rain
It is by the unfailing fall of rain that the earth sustaineth itself: therefore is the rain called the immortal drink.
Every food that is sweet to the taste is given to man by Rain: and itself formeth also part of his food.
It rain should fail, famine would rage over the wide earth even though it is encircled by the ocean.
Husbandmen would cease to ply the plough if the fountains of the heavens are dried up.
It is rain that ruineth, and it is rain again that setteth up those that it hath ruined.
Even grass will cease to grow if the showers from above should cease to fall.
Even the mighty ocean would reek with corruption if the heavens should cease to suck its waters and render them back to it.
Sacrifices will not be offered to the Gods nor Feasts be celebrated on earth if the heavens are dried up.
Neither charity nor austerities will abide on the wide earth if the heavens should hold back their showers.
Nothing on earth can go on without water: so even right conduct itself depends ultimately on rain.
III
The Greatness of Those Who Have Renounced the World
Behold the men who have renounced sense-enjoyments and live a life of discipline: the scriptures exalt their glory above every other good.
Thou canst not measure the greatness of ascetics: thou canst as well count the number of the dead.
Behold the men who have weighed this life with the next and have renounced: the earth is made radiant by their greatness.
Behold the man whose firm will controlleth his five senses even as the goading hook controlleth the elephant: he is a seed fit for the fields of heaven.
The King of the Gods himself, Indra, is witness unto the might of him that hath burned away the five desires.5
The great ones are they who can achieve the impossible:6 the feeble ones are those who cannot.
Behold the man who appreciateth at their true value the sensations of touch and taste and sight and sound and smell:7 he will command the world.
The scriptures of the world proclaim the greatness of the men of the mighty word.
It is impossible to support even for a second the wrath of those who stand on the rock of renunciation.
It is saintly men that are to be called Brahmans: for it is they that have compassion on all life.8
IV
The Glorification of Righteousness
Righteousness leadeth unto heaven and it bringeth wealth also: what is there that is more profitable than Righteousness?
There is no greater good than Righteousness, nor no greater ill than the forgetting of it.
Be thou unremitting in the doing of good deeds: do them with all thy might and by every means.
Be pure in heart: all righteousness is contained in this one commandment: all other things are nought but empty sound.
Avoid envy and greed, anger and harsh words: that is the way to acquire righteousness.
Say not in thy heart, I shall be righteous by and bye, but begin to do good works without delaying: for it is Righteousness will be thy undying companion on the day of thy death.
Ask me not, Where is the good of Righteousness? Look at the bearer of the palanquin and him that rideth on it.9
If thou do good all thy life without a single waste day, thou wallest up the road to future births.
That alone is delight which cometh of Righteousness: all else is pain and shame.
That action alone is worth doing which is righteous: and all action must be shunned which is unrighteous.

The Life of the Householder
V
Family Life
The householder is the mainstay of all who follow the three other paths of life.10
The householder is the friend of the orphan and the pauper and the helpless dead.11

Five are the duties of the householder, namely, the offering of oblations to the dead, the performance of sacrifices to the Gods, the doing of hospitality, the rendering of help unto relations, and the looking after of one’s own self.
Behold the man who feareth to do ill and doth charity before eating his meal: his seed decayeth never.
If love aboundeth in the home and righteousness doth prevail, the home is perfect and its end is all fulfilled.
If a man fulfilleth aright the duties of the householder, where is the need for him to take up other duties?
Among those that seek after salvation the greatest are they who lead a virtuous family life.
Behold the householder who helpeth others in the observance of their vows and who leadeth a virtuous life himself: he is holier than the austere ones themselves.
Righteousness belongeth especially to the married life: and a good name is its ornament.
The householder who liveth as he ought to live will be looked upon as a God among men.
VI
The Blessings of a Good Helpmate
She is the good helpmate who possesseth every wifely virtue and spendeth not above her husband’s means.
All other blessings turn to nought if the wife faileth in wifely virtues.
Where is indigence if the wife is worthy? and where is riches is worth is not in her?
What is there that is grander than woman, when she is strong in the strength of her chastity?
Behold the woman who worshippeth not other Gods but worshippeth her husband even as she riseth from bed: the rain-cloud obeyeth her commands.
She is the good housewife who guardeth her virtue and her reputation, and tendeth her husband with loving care.
Of what avail is close confinement? It is her own continence that is the best guardian of a woman’s virtue.
Behold the woman who hath begotten a worthy son: her place is high in the world of the Gods.
Behold the man whose home beareth not an honourable reputation: the proud lion-like walk in the sight of detractors is denied him.
The chiefest blessing is an honourable home: and its crowning glory is worthy offspring.
VII
Offspring
We know of no blessing so great as the begetting of children that are endowed with understanding.
Behold the man whose children bear an unstained character: no evil will touch him in any of his seven reincarnations.
Children are the veritable riches of a man: for they pass to him by their own acts all the merits that they acquire.
Sweeter verily than ambrosia is the plain soup bespattered by the tender hands of one’s own children.
The touch of children is the delight of the body: the delight of the ear is the hearing of their speech.
The flute is sweet and the guitar dulcet: so say they who have not heard the babbling speech of their little ones.
What is the duty of the father to his son? It is to make him worthy to sit in the front rank in the assembly.
To find oneself eclipsed in intelligence by one’s children is a delight to all the world.
Great is the joy of the mother when a male child is born unto her: but greater far is her delight when she heareth him called worthy.
What is the duty of the son to his father? It is to make the world ask, For what austerities of his hath he been blessed with such a son?
VIII
Love
Where is the bar that can close in the gates of love? The gentle teardrops of lovers’ eyes are sure to proclaim its presence.
Those that love not live only for themselves: as to those that love, their very bones are for others’ occasions.
They say it is to taste again of love that the soul hath consented once more to be encased in bone.
Love maketh the heart tender towards all: and tenderness yieldeth that priceless treasure called friendship.
The blessing of the blessed, they say, is only the reward of a constant love.
They are fools who say that love is for the righteous alone: for even against the evil-minded love is the only ally for a man.
Behold how the sun burneth the boneless worm: even so doth Righteousness burn the man that doth not love.
Behold the man that loveth not: he will know prosperity only when the sapless tree of the desert putteth forth leaves.
Of what avail is a lovely outside, if love, the soul’s ornament, hath no place in the heart?
The seat of life is in Love: who hath it not is only a mass of skin-encased bone.
IX
Hospitality
What for do the wise toil and set up homes? It is to feed the guest and help the pilgrim.
Were it even the draught of immortality, it shall not be tasted alone when the guest is in the hall.
No evil befalleth the man who never faileth to honour the incoming guest.
Behold the man who receiveth the worthy guest with his best smile: Lakshmi12 delighteth to abide in his home.
Behold the man who feedeth his guest first and then only eateth what is left: standeth his land in need even of sowing?
Behold the man who hath tended the outgoing guest and waiteth for the incoming one: he is a welcome guest unto the Gods.
We cannot say of any hospitable act by itself, So much is the merit of this act: it is the worth of the guest that is the measure of the sacrifice.
Behold the man who performeth not the sacrifice of hospitality: he will say one day, I have toiled hard and laid me up a great treasure: but it is all in vain, for there is none to comfort me.
Not to honour the pilgrim is veritable indigence in the midst of wealth: such a thing is found only with fools.
The anitcha flower fadeth by smelling: but a look is enough to break the heart of the guest.
X
Kindness of Speech
The speech that is truly kind is the speech of the righteous men which is full of tenderness and free from dissimulation.
Better even than a generous gift is sweet speech and a kind and gracious look.
Behold the sweet and gracious look and the kind speech that cometh from the heart: Righteousness hath its dwelling place there.
Behold the man who always speaketh words which gladden all hearts: Poverty, the increaser of sorrow, will never come to him.
Modesty and a loving speech, these alone are the ornaments of man and none other.
Sinfulness will wane away and righteousness will increase if thy thoughts are good and thy speech is kind.
The word that is serviceable and kind createth friends and bringeth forth benefits.
Words that are kind and are removed from all littleness yield good in this life and in the next also.
Why doth not a man cease from violent words, even after he hath felt the sweetness that kind words give?
Behold the man who useth hard words when sweet ones serve: he preferreth the unripe fruit to the ripe.
XI
Gratitude
Behold the kindness done without any obligation: even the heavens and the earth are too poor to repay it.
A kindness done in the hour of need may look small: but it outweigheth the whole world.
Behold the kindness done without thought of recompense: it is mightier than the ocean.
The benefit received may be small even like a millet seed: but in the eyes of the just its measure is that of a palmyra tree.
Gratitude is not limited by the assistance given: it is bounded only by the nobility of him that receiveth it.
Disregard not the friendship of the holy ones: forsake not those that succoured thee in difficulty.
He that hath relieved from affliction shall be remembered with gratitude in every birth.
It is ignoble to forget a kindness: but an ill turn received it is the part of nobility to forget at once.
The mortallest injury is forgiven the moment the mind recalleth a single kindness received from the injurer.
There is redemption for men who are guilty of every other crime: but the ingrate wretch shall know of none.
XII
Uprightness of Heart
The just and the fair that giveth each man his due whether he is friend or foe, that is the good: nought else.
The prosperity of the just groweth not less: it endureth even unto their remotest posterity.
Though nought but profit come of it, touch not the wealth that cometh by deviating from the right.
The righteous and the unrighteous are known by their offspring.
Evil and good come unto all: but an upright heart is the glory of the wise.
When thy heart swerveth from the right and turneth unto evil, know that thy destruction is near at hand.
The world looketh not down on the poverty of the upright and virtuous man.
Behold the weighing beam, for it is straight in itself and weigheth justly: the glory of the wise is to be like unto it and to incline neither to this side nor to that.
Behold the man who swerveth not at all from the right in his own mind: the upright speech of his lips is a judgment.
Behold the businessman that looketh after the interests of others as his own: his business will expand.
XIII
Self-Control
Self-control leadeth unto heaven, but uncontrolled passion is the royal road to endless darkness.
Guard thy self-control as a very treasure: life hath no richer wealth here below.
Behold the man who controlleth his passions consciously and by the right way: wisdom and every other blessing will come unto him.
Behold the man who hath triumphed over his passions and who swerveth not from duty: his form is more imposing than a mountain.
Humility is beautiful in all man: but alone on the rich doth it shine in all its splendour.
Behold the man who can draw in into himself his five senses even as the tortoise doth its limbs: he hath laid up for himself a treasure for all his future births.
Whatever else thou rein not in, rein in thy tongue: for an unbridled tongue leadeth unto grief.
If even one word of thine causeth pain to another, all thy virtue is lost.
The burn caused by fire healeth in its time: but the wound burned in by the tongue remaineth green forever.
Behold the man who hath learned wisdom and whose mind is tranquil and under perfect control: Righteousness pilgrimageth to his home in order to have a look at him.
XIV
Purity of Conduct
The man whose conduct is pure is honoured by all: purity of conduct is therefore to be prized even above life.
Watch anxiously over thy conduct: for wheresoever thou mayest search thou canst not find a firmer ally than right conduct.
Good conduct bespeaketh an honourable family: but low conduct placeth a man amongst the ignoble.
Even the Vedas if forgotten can be learned again: but once fallen from virtuous conduct the Brahman is fallen from his place forever.
Prosperity is not for the envious: even so dignity is not for men of ill conduct.
The firm-minded swerve not from virtuous conduct: for they know the evils brought on by such swerving.
The man of right conduct is honoured among men: but ignominy alone is the portion of those who fall therefrom.
Good conduct soweth the seed of prosperity: but an evil course is the mother of endless ills.
Foul words can never fall from the lips of the well-bred even when off their guard.
Fools may be as instructed as thou pleasest: but they never learn to conform to the ways of the Righteous.
XV
Non-Desiring of Another Man’s Wife
Behold the men whose eyes are turned towards righteousness and towards wealth: they commit not the folly of desiring another man’s wife.
Among those that have fallen from virtue there is no greater fool than he that standeth at his neighbour’s threshold.
Verily they are in the jaws of death who invade the home of an unsuspecting friend.
Let a man be ever so great: what availeth it all if he committeth adultery without thinking ever so little of the shame that floweth therefrom?
Behold the man who hangeth on to his neighbour’s wife because she is accessible: his name is sullied forever.
The adulterer knoweth no respite from four things, hatred, sin, fear, and shame.
He is the righteous householder who careth not for the charms of his neighbour’s wife.
Behold the high-souled man that looketh not on another’s wife: he is more than righteous: he is saintly.
Who on earth deserve all the good things of the world? It is they who clasp not the arms of her who belongeth to another.
Though thou shouldst transgress and yield to every other sin, it were well for thee if thou desire not thy neighbour’s wife.
XVI
Forgiveness
The earth supporteth even those that dig into her: even so bear thou with those that traduce thee; for that is greatness.
Forgive thou always the injuries that others may do thee: but if thou forget them, it were even better.
The most shameful poverty is the refusal of hospitality: and the greatest strength is to bear with the dullness of fools.
If thou want to be grand always, be forgiving unto all.
The wise respect not the men who retaliate an injury: but they are prized as gold who forgive their enemy.
The joy of revenge lasteth but a day: but the glory of him who forgiveth endureth forever.
Be the wrong suffered ever so great: the better part is not to take it to heart and to abstain from revenge.
Conquer by thy nobility those that in their pride have injured thee.
More saintly than even those that have renounced are they that bear with the bitter tongue of their detractors.
Those that do penance by fasting are great: but they only come after those that forgive their calumniators.
XVII
Non-Envying
Guard thyself from envious thoughts: for freedom from envy is a part of virtuous conduct.
No blessing is so great as a nature that is free from all envy.
It is he that careth not for virtue or for wealth that envieth his neighbour’s prosperity.
The wise injure not others through envy: for they know the evils that result therefrom.
Envy itself is scourge enough for the envious man: for, even if his enemies spare him, his own envy will work his ruin.
Behold the man that beareth not to see gifts made to another: his family will beg for very food and clothing and perish.
Lakshmi13 cannot bear with the envious: she will abandon them to the care of her elder sister14 and quit their side.
Caitiff Envy bringeth on indigence and leadeth up to the gates of hell.
The affluence of the envious and the misery of the generous-minded are alike matter for wonder.
Never hath envy led to prosperity: nor a liberal heart to a fall therefrom.
XVIII
Non-Coveting
Behold the man who leaveth the right way and coveteth another man’s wealth: his wickednesses will increase and his family will decline.
Behold the men that turn away from evil: they covet not, neither do they yield to ignoble deeds.
Behold the men that care for other joys: they are not greedy after little delights, nor do they yield unto iniquity.
Behold the men that have mastered their senses and enlarged their vision: they covet not saying, Lo, we are in want.
Of what avail is a mind that is subtle and comprehending, if it yieldeth unto greed and consenteth unto insensate deeds?
Even he who hungereth after grace and walketh in the path shall perish if he hankereth after wealth and plotteth evil.
Covet not the wealth that greed gathereth: for its fruit is bitter in the day of enjoyment.
If thou desire that thy substance should not grow less, covet not the riches in thy neighbour’s hands.
Behold the wise man that understandeth justice and coveteth not: Lakshmi knoweth his worth and seeketh him in his home.
The greed that looketh not beyond engendereth destruction: but the greatness that sayeth, I desire not, triumpheth over all.
XIX
Refraining from Slander
Behold the man who doeth iniquity and who speaketh not so much as the name of righteousness: it is sweet even unto him if men say, Lo, here is one who backbiteth not.
It is wrong to turn away from good and do evil: but it is far worse to smile before and vilify behind.
It is worthier to die at once than live by lying and slander: for such a death bringeth with it the fruits of righteousness.
Slander not a man behind his back even though he hath insulted thee to thy very face.
The lips may speak righteousness: but a slanderous tongue betrayeth the meanness of the heart.
If thou slander another, he will look into thy own transgressions and expose the worst of them.
They that know not to speak sweet and to make friendships create discord and separate men who were friends.
Those that speak abroad the transgressions of their friends, how will they spare the transgressions of their enemies?
How doth the Earth suffer patiently the tread of the calumniator on her bosom? Is it that she looketh unto Righteousness to rid her of him?
If a man can scan his own faults as he doth those of his enemies, can evil ever come to him?
XX
Refraining from Vain Speaking
Behold the man that angereth the public by the speaking of vain words: he will be despised of all men.
Worse even than injuring one’s friends is the speaking of vain words before many.
He that multiplieth empty words declareth loud his want of worth.
Behold the man that speaketh vain words in an assembly: no profit will come unto him and all that is good will flee from his side.
Even the worthy will lose honour and respect if they indulge in vain speaking.
Call not him man who loveth idle words: call him rather a chaff among men.
Let the wise, if they deem it meet, speak even hard words: but it is good for them to desist from profitless speech.
The wise whose thoughts are set on great questions utter not words that are profitless and vain.
They whose eyes are whole say not vain words even by oversight.
Speak thou the speech that bringeth forth profit: but speak not ever words that are profitless and vain.
XXI
Fear of Evildoing
The evil fear not the folly called sin: but the worthy flee from it.
Evil bringeth forth evil: evil therefore shall be feared even more than fire.
The chiefest wisdom, they say, is to abstain from injury even to an enemy.
Let not a man compass another’s ruin even by oversight: for Justice will compass the ruin of him that plotteth evil.
Let not a man work evil saying, I am poor: for, if he do, he will sink into a lower destitution than before.
Whoso desireth not to be saddened by ills, let him abstain from doing injury to others.
There is a way of escape from every other enemy: but ill deeds never die but pursue and destroy their author.
As the shadow leaveth not a man but doggeth his steps wherever he goeth, even so do evil deeds pursue their author and work his destruction.
If a man love his own self, let him not incline toward evil in any degree.
Know that man to be secure from ills who leaveth not the straight path in order to commit wrong.
XXII
Complaisance
The gracious expect no return when they oblige: how ever can the world repay the rain-cloud?
The substance gathered in by the worthy by the labour of their hands is all for others’ use.
A better thing than a gracious complaisance cannot be had either here or in heaven.
He alone liveth who knoweth what is proper: he who knoweth not what is fitting shall be classed with the dead.
Behold the village tank filled with water to its brim: like unto it is the prosperity of the wise man that loveth the world.
Like unto a fruit-tree in the middle of the village bearing fruit is riches in the hands of the man of heart.
Like unto a tree that yieldeth medicinal drugs and drieth not is riches in the hands of the generous man.
Behold the men who know what is just and proper: they fail not to oblige others even when fallen on evil days.
The complaisant man thinketh himself poor only when he is impotent to oblige those who solicit his aid.
If ruin cometh as a result of complaisance, it is worth courting even by selling one’s own self into slavery.
XXIII
Charity
Giving to the poor is alone charity: all other giving is of the nature of loan.
Though it lead unto heaven, receiving is bad: and though heaven should be denied to the giver, giving alms is a virtue.
It is only the highborn man that giveth without ever meanly saying, I have not.
The heart of the giver is not glad until he seeth the smile of content on the face of the suppliant.
The conquest of conquests to the conqueror over self is the conquest over hunger: but his conquest cometh only after the conquest of him who appeaseth that hunger.15
To fill the gnawing hunger of the poor: that is the way that the wealthy man should lay up riches for himself.
The evil disease called hunger toucheth not the man that divideth his bread with others.
The hard of heart who perish their wealth by hoarding it, have not they ever tasted the delight of giving unto others?
Bitterer verily than the beggar’s bread is the hoarded meal of the miser eating alone.
Nothing is bitterer than death: but even death is sweet when one hath not the power to do charity.
XXIV
Glory
Give to the poor and add glory unto thy name: there is no greater profit for man than this.
The one theme in the mouth of all that praise is the glory of those that give unto the poor.
Everything else dieth on earth: but the fame that hath no rival endureth forever.
Behold the man that hath won a lasting, worldwide fame: the Gods on high prefer him even before saints.
The ruin that addeth unto fame and the death that bringeth glory belong only to the great-souled.
If men must needs be born into the world, let them earn glory: as to those who earn it not, it were better for them not to have been born at all.
Those that are not free from blemish chafe not at themselves: why then are they wroth against their calumniators?
It is a disgrace for all men if they earn not the memory called fame.
Behold the land weighed down beneath the tread of an inglorious people: its riches, even though renowned in the past, will wane away.
They alone live who live without blemish: and they alone die who have lived without glory.
Section II
The Life of the Ascetic
Subdivision A
Discipline
XXV
Mercy
The chiefest wealth is a heart that is rich in mercy: for material wealth is found even in the hands of vile men.
Reason by the right method and take up Mercy: and if thou inquire of all religions also, thou shalt see that Mercy is the only salvation.
They enter not into the dark and bitter world whose heart is joined unto mercy.
The results of actions at which the soul trembleth pursue not him who is kind and merciful to all life.
Affliction is not for the merciful: the teeming air-encircled earth is a witness thereto.
Behold the man that hath forsaken mercy and doth iniquity: though he must have suffered cruelly in past births for abandoning virtue, he hath forgotten the lesson, say the wise.
The other world is not for those that have not mercy, even as this world is not for them that are without riches.
The poor in substance may one day thrive and prosper: but they that lack pity are poor indeed and their day cometh never.
It is as easy for the hard of heart to do deeds of righteousness as for the confused in mind to realise the Truth.
When thou art tempted to oppress the weak, consider how it would be for thee to tremble before a stronger.
XXVI
Abjuring of Flesh-Meat
How can he feel pity, who eateth other flesh in order to fatten his own?
Riches are not for the thriftless: even so pity is not for those that eat meat.
The heart of the man that tasteth flesh turneth not towards good, even as the heart of him that is armed with steel.
The killing of animals is veritable hardness of heart: but the eating of their flesh is iniquity indeed.
In non-eating of flesh is Life: if thou eat, the pit of hell will not open its mouth to let thee out.
If the world desireth not meat for eating, there will be none to offer it for sale.
If a man can only realise to himself the agony and pain suffered by other living beings, he would not desire to eat flesh-meat.
Behold the men who have escaped from the bonds of illusion and ignorance: they eat not the flesh from which life hath flown out.
To abstain from the killing and eating of living things is better than to perform a thousand sacrifices in the sacrificial fire.
Behold the man who killeth not and abstaineth from flesh-meat: all the world joineth hands to do him reverence.
XXVII
Tapas16
Patient endurance of suffering and non-injuring of life, in these is contained the whole of tapas.
Austerities are for the austere of heart: it is profitless for others to take them up.
Is it because there should be some people to tend and feed ascetics that all the rest have forgotten tapas?
It thou wouldst destroy thy foes and exalt those that love thee, know that such a power belongeth unto tapas.
Tapas fulfilleth all desires even in the very manner that is desired: therefore is it that men endeavour after tapas in this world.
It is the men that do tapas that look after their own interests: the rest are caught in the snares of desire and only do themselves harm.
The fiercer the fire in which it is melted the more brilliant becometh the lustre of the gold: even so the severer the sufferings endured by the austere, the purer their nature shineth.
Behold the man who hath attained mastery over himself: all other men worship him.
Behold the men that have acquired power by austerities: they can succeed even in conquering death.
If the needy are the many in the world, it is because those that do tapas are few, and those that do not, the larger number.
XXVIII
Imposture
The five17 principles of his own body smile within themselves when they see the imposture of the hypocrite.
Of what avail is an imposing presence when evil is in the heart and the heart is conscious thereof?
Behold the ungodly man putting on the puissant look of the austere: he is like a cow that grazeth about wearing a tiger’s skin.
Behold the man who taketh cover under a saintly garb and doth evil: he is like a fowler hiding in the bush and catching birds.
The hypocrite pretendeth unto sanctity and sayeth, I have vanquished my passions: but he will come to grief and cry, What have I done? and what have I done?
Behold the man that hath not renounced in his heart, but walketh about like one that hath renounced, and cheateth men: there is none more hard of heart than he.
The kunri seed is fair on one side, but the other side of it is black: there are men who are like unto it: they are fair on the outside, but their inside is all black.
Many there be whose heart is impure but who bathe in holy streams and prowl about.
The arrow is straight and the lute hath a bend: judge thou therefore men by their acts and not by their appearance.
Neither matted hair thou wantest nor shaven head, if thou abstain from that which the world contemneth.
XXIX
Abstaining from Fraud
Whoso wanteth not to be held in contempt, let him guard himself against every thought of fraud.
It is a sin even to say in one’s heart, I shall cheat my neighbour of his substance.
The fortune that is built up by fraud may appear to thrive; but it is doomed forever.
The thirst for plunder leadeth in its season to endless grief.
Behold the man that coveteth other men’s substance and lieth in wait to catch them napping: he thinketh not of grace and love is far from his heart.
The man who thirsteth after plunder cannot weigh things aright: nor can he walk in the way of righteousness.
Behold the man that hath weighed the things of this world and made his heart firm: he committeth not the folly of cheating his neighbour.
As Righteousness resideth in the heart of him who valueth things aright, even so Deceit hath its seat in the heart of the thief.
Behold the man who meditateth on nothing but theft and plunder: he will leave the right path and perish.
He that deceiveth others is not master even of his own body: but the world of the Gods itself is a never-failing inheritance unto the men that are righteous.
XXX
Truthfulness
What is truthfulness? It is the speaking of that which is free from even the slightest taint of evil.
Even falsehood is of the nature of truth if it bringeth forth unmixed good.18
Bear not false witness against thy neighbour: for thy own conscience will burn thee when thou hast lied.
Behold the man whose heart is free from falsehood: he reigneth in the hearts of all.
Behold the man whose heart is fixed in truthfulness: he is greater than the austere and greater than he that distributeth alms.
There is no greater renown for a man than the renown that he is a stranger unto falsehood: such a man obtaineth every blessing without mortifying the body.
If a map can live without ever uttering a falsehood, all other virtue is superfluous unto him.
The cleanliness of the body belongeth unto water: but the purity of the heart is proved by truthfulness.
The worthy regard not all other light as light: it is only the light of truth that they look upon as a veritable illumination.
Many things have I seen in this world: but of all the things that I have seen, there is nothing that is higher than truth.
XXXI
Abstaining from Anger
He alone can be said to forbear who hath the power to strike: as to him that hath not the power, what mattereth it whether he forbeareth or forbeareth not?
It is wrong to get angry even when thou art helpless to strike: and when thou hast the power, there is nothing that is worse than anger.
Whoever thy offender may be, forget thy anger: for from anger springeth a multitude of ills.
Anger killeth the smile and it destroyeth cheer: hath man a crueller foe than anger?
If thou want to look after thyself, keep off from choler: for if thou keep not off, it will come upon thee and destroy thy own self.
Choler destroyeth every man whom it approacheth: and it burneth also the family of him who nurseth it.

He who nurseth his rage as if it were a precious thing is like unto the man who dasheth his hand against the ground: the hand of this man escapeth not from injury, and the destruction of the first is as certain.
Even when thy wrongs burn as the flaming of many fires, it is good if thou canst abstain from anger.
All the desires of a man will be fulfilled on the instant if from his heart he banish anger.
Whoso is overwhelmed with anger is like one dead: but whoso hath forsworn wrathfulness is like unto the saints.
XXXII
Non-Injuring
The pure in heart injure not others even for the sake of the wealth that glorifieth a man: for that is their way.
Even when another hath injured them in his hate, the pure in heart return not the injury: for that is their way.
If thou injure another, even though it be only a man who hath injured thee without any provocation, thou simply bringest down upon thyself evils that can never be remedied.
How shall a man punish them that have injured him? Let him do them a good turn and make them ashamed in their hearts.
Of what avail is intelligence to a man if he doth not look on others’ pain as his own and abstain from injuring any?
When a man hath felt a pain for himself, let him take care that he inflicteth it not on others.
It is a great thing it thou injure not knowingly any man, at any time, and in any degree.
He who hath felt what pain meaneth to himself, how doth he bring himself to inflict it on others?
If a man injureth his neighbour in the forenoon, evil will come to him in the afternoon of its own accord.
All evil recoileth on the head of the wrongdoer: they abstain therefore from wrongdoing who desire to be immune from ills.
XXXIII
Non-Killing
The greatest of virtues is non-killing: killing bringeth in its train every other sin.
To divide one’s bread with the needy and to abstain from killing: this is the greatest of all the commandments of all the prophets.
The greatest virtue of all is non-killing: truthfulness cometh only next.
What is the good way? It is the path that taketh thought how it may save even the smallest of creatures from being killed.
Among all that have renounced this life with its fears of ill, the chiefest is he that reverenceth all life for fear of killing any.
Behold the man who hath taken the vow of non-killing: Death that eateth away all life maketh no inroads into his days.
Take not away from any living thing the life that is sweet unto all, even if it be to save thine own.
They may say, Sacrifices gain for a man many blessings: but to the pure in heart the blessings that are earned by killing are an abomination.
Those who live by slaying are likened by the discriminating to eaters of carrion.
Behold the man whose putrid body is festering with ulcerous sores: he must have been a shedder of blood in the past, say the wise.
Subdivision B
Wisdom
XXXIV
The Vanity of All Things
There is no greater folly than the infatuation that looketh upon the transient as if it were everlasting.
The crowd that assembleth to witness a village show, that is the symbol of great riches flowing on a man: and the dispersal of that same crowd is the type of its passing away.
Prosperity is transient: if thou have come by it, delay not to do things that are of lasting good.
Tine looketh like an innocent thing: but verily it is a saw that is continually sawing away the life of man.
Make haste to do good works before the tongue is paralysed and hiccup ariseth in the throat.
But yesterday a man was and today he is not: that is the wonder of wonders in this world.
Man knoweth not if he shall last the next minute: but his thoughts are more than ten million.
The fledgeling abandoneth the broken shell of the egg and flieth away: that is the symbol of the love between the soul and the body.
Death is like unto a sleep: and life is like the waking after that sleep.
Hath the soul no home of its own, that it taketh shelter in this worthless body?
XXXV
Renunciation
Whatsoever thing a man hath renounced, from the grief arising from that thing hath he liberated himself.
If thou want joy, renounce early: for many are the delights that thou shalt enjoy after renouncing.
Crush thou the five senses: and everything in which thou takest delight, give up utterly.
To possess nothing, that is the law of the man of vows: the possession of even one thing is a coming back to the snares that he hath left.
To those that desire to put an end to their reincarnations, even the body is a superfluity: how much more then are other bonds?
The feelings of I and Mine are nought but vanity and pride: he who crusheth them entereth a higher world than the world of the Gods.
Behold the man who holdeth on to attachments and giveth not them up: Grief shall take hold of him and shall not give him up.
They that have renounced utterly are on the path to salvation: but the others are caught in a snare.
The moment that attachments are broken, that very moment reincarnations cease: the man who breaketh them not continueth in vanity.
Take thou refuge in Him who hath conquered all attachments: and hold fast to that ark in order that all thy bonds may be broken.
XXXVI
Realisation of the Truth
From the delusion of taking vanities for the Reality a man cometh by a life of sorrow.
Behold the man who is freed from delusion and who hath an unclouded vision: darkness ceaseth for him and joy cometh unto him.
Behold the man who hath freed himself from uncertainties and who hath realised the Truth: heaven is nearer to him than the earth.
Though risen to human birth, nought is gained if the soul realiseth not the Truth.
To separate the true from the false in everything, whatever its nature may be, that is the part of a wise understanding.
Behold the man who hath studied deeply and hath realised the Truth: he shall enter the path that leadeth not again into this world.
Verily those that have meditated upon and attained to the Truth need not think at all of future incarnations.
It is the part of Wisdom to desire to escape the folly called birth, and to aim at realising the Supreme and the Good.
Behold the man who understandeth the means of his salvation and laboureth to conquer all attachments: the ills that he is yet to suffer depart from him.
As desire and anger and delusion leave a man, his ills also follow their pace and slowly melt away.
XXXVII
The Killing of Desire
Desire is the seed that yieldeth unto every soul, and always, a never-failing crop of births.
If thou must needs long for anything, long for freedom from reincarnation: and that freedom shall come to thee if thou long to conquer longing.
There is no greater wealth here below than desirelessness: and wherever thou goest thou canst find no treasure that equalleth it.
Purity is nought but freedom from desire: and this freedom is achieved by yearning for perfect truthfulness.
It is those that have conquered their desire that are called the liberated ones: the others appear to be free but they are verily in bondage.
If thou love righteousness, flee from desire: for desire is a snare and a disappointment.
If a man cutteth off utterly all his desires, salvation shall come to him by any path that he commandeth to it.
He that hath no desires hath no grief: but ills on ills descend on the man that hankereth after things.
Even here a man shall have everlasting joy if he killeth that greatest misery of all, desire.
Desire is never filled: but if a man giveth it up he attaineth perfection even at that very moment.
XXXVIII
Destiny
Resolution cometh to a man when Fortune is about to smile on him; but Indolence appeareth when Fortune is about to leave.
Evil fate dulleth the faculties: but when Fortune is about to smile she first expandeth the intelligence.
What doth learning avail and all subtleties? It is the Spirit that is inside that prevaileth over all.
There are two things in the world which have nothing in common: Riches is one thing and Saintliness is quite another.
When the tide is against thee even good things turn to evil: and even evil things turn to good when the tide is on.
What Destiny denieth thou canst not keep even with the utmost care: and even if thou scatter abroad, the things that are thine will not go away from thee.
Even the man who hath amassed ten million cannot enjoy his riches except as the Ordainer hath ordained.
Verily the destitute poor would turn their hearts towards renunciation but that Destiny reserveth them for the miseries that are their portion.
He that rejoiceth when good cometh, why should he fret when he receiveth evil?
What is there that is mightier than Destiny? For even as its victim is meditating a plan to overcome it, it forestalleth him and bringeth him down.
Part II
Wealth
Section I
The Prince
XXXIX
The Qualifications of the Prince
He is a lion among princes who is well endowed in respect of the six things: troops, population, substance, council, alliances, and fortifications.
Four qualities should never be wanting in the prince, namely, courage, liberality, wisdom, and energy.
Behold the men that are destined to rule the earth: the three virtues, alertness, learning, and decision, leave them not.
The prince shall not fail in virtue and shall abolish unrighteousness: he shall guard his honour jealously but shall not sin against the laws of valour.
The prince shall know how to develop the resources of his kingdom and how to enrich his treasury: how to preserve his wealth and how to spend it worthily.
If the prince is accessible to all his subjects and is never harsh of word, his kingdom will be esteemed above every other.
Behold the prince who can give with grace and rule with love: his name will fill the world.
Behold the prince who administereth impartial justice and protecteth his subjects: he shall be called a God among men.
Behold the prince who hath the virtue to bear with words that are bitter to the ear: the world will rest permanently under his umbrella.
Behold the prince who is liberal and gracious and just, and who tendeth his people with care: he is a light among kings.
XL
Learning
Acquire thoroughly the knowledge that is worth acquiring and after acquiring it walk thou in accordance therewith.
Two are the eyes of living kind: the one is called Numbers, and the other, Letters.
The learned alone can be said to possess eyes: the unlettered have but two sores in their head.
The scholar bringeth joy with him wherever he cometh: but when he departeth he leaveth regrets behind.
Though thou hast to humble thyself before the teacher even as a beggar before a man of wealth thou yet acquirest learning: it is those that refuse to learn that are the lowest among men.
Knowledge is like unto a sand-spring: the more thou diggest and drawest thereat, the more excellent is the flow thereof.
Everywhere is his home to the learned man, and everywhere his native land: why then doth a man neglect instruction up to his dying day?
The learning that a man hath acquired in one birth will exalt him; even in all his succeeding incarnations.
The learned man seeth that the learning that delighteth him delighteth also all that listen to him: and he loveth instruction all the more on that account.
An imperishable and flawless treasure is learning to a man: other wealth is as nothing before it.
XLI
The Neglecting of Instruction
Ascending the rostrum without abundant knowledge is like the playing of dice without the chequered board.19
Behold the man without learning who desireth to be called eloquent: he is like unto a woman without busts who yearneth to be admired of men.
Even a fool shall be counted wise if he can hold his peace before the learned.
The opinion of an ignorant man will be rejected by the wise even though it may be perfectly sensible.
Behold the ignorant man who is wise in his own eyes: he will be put to shame directly he openeth his lips in an assembly.
Like unto a wasteland that yieldeth no harvests is the man that hath neglected instruction: all that men can say about him is that he liveth, and nothing more.
Behold the man whose understanding hath not been penetrated by the Grand and the Subtle: the comeliness of his person is no better than the beauty of an image of clay.
Bitter verily is the poverty of the man of learning: but far worse is riches in the hands of the fool.
The fool though born of a higher family is esteemed much less than a learned man who is of inferior descent.
How much better are men than beasts? Even so much are the learned better than those that have not cared for instruction.
XLII
Listening to the Instruction of the Wise
The most precious of treasures is the treasure of the ear: verily it is the crown of all kinds of wealth.
Even unto the stomach some food will be offered when there is no more food to be offered to the ear.20
Behold the men who have listened to much instruction: they are very Gods on earth.
Let a man hear instruction even though he hath no learning: for it will be a stay unto him when he is encompassed by difficulty.
The counsel of the righteous is like unto a strong staff: for it keepeth those that listen to it from slipping.
Listen to good words though they be but few: even those few will add to thee a proportionate dignity.
Behold the man that hath meditated much in himself and hath laid by a store of instruction by listening to the wise: he talketh not nonsense even when in error.
Deaf indeed though it heareth is the ear that hath not been drilled by words of instruction.
Humility of speech is hard to be attained by those who have not listened to the subtle words of the wise.
Behold the men that taste with the tongue but know not the taste of the ear: what doth it matter to the world whether they live or die?
XLIII
The Understanding
The understanding is an armour against all surprise: it is a fortress which even enemies cannot storm.
It is the understanding that curbeth the senses from roving about, keepeth them from evil, and directeth them towards the Good.
To separate the true from the false in every utterance, whoever it be that speaketh, that is the part of a wise understanding.
What he speaketh, the wise man speaketh so as to be understood by all: and from the lips of others he gathereth their subtle meanings.
The wise man is sociable with all the world: and his temper is ever even, expanding not nor contracting to excess.
It is a part of wisdom to conform to the ways of the world.
The man of understanding knoweth what is coming: but the fool foreseeth not what is before.
It is folly to rush headlong into danger: it is the part of the wise to fear what ought to be feared.
Behold the man of foresight who is armed for every contingency: he will never know the blow that causeth trembling.
He that hath understanding hath everything: but the fool though he possess everything hath nothing.
XLIV
Eschewing of Faults
Behold the man who is free from haughtiness and anger and the vulgar passion:21 there is a dignity about him that adorneth his prosperity.
Parsimony, overconfidence, and excessive amour propre are faults in the prince.
Behold the men who are jealous of their reputation: though their fault be small even like a millet seed, they look upon it as of the measure of a palmyra tree.
Guard thyself jealously against weaknesses: for they are the foes that will lead thee to ruin.
Behold the man who provideth not beforehand against surprise: he will be destroyed even like a stack of straw before a spark of fire.
If the prince correcteth his own faults and then looketh into those of others, where is the ill that can approach him?
Behold the miser that spendeth not where he ought to spend: his wealth will come to an inglorious wreck.
Closefisted parsimony is not a vice to be classed with other vices: it formeth a class apart.
Exult not at anything at any time: embark not on enterprises that would bring thee no good.
If thou canst keep from the knowledge of others the things in which thy heart taketh delight, the machinations of thy foes will be in vain.
XLV
Courting the Friendship of the Worthy
Esteem thou the men that have grown old in righteousness, and acquire their friendship.
Behold the men who can cure the evils that have already befallen thee and who can guard thee from future ones: cultivate thou their friendship with ardour.
It is the rarest of rare good fortunes if a man can secure to himself the devotion of men of worth.
If those that are worthier than thyself have become thy intimates, thou hast acquired a strength before which all other strength paleth.
As the eyes of the prince are his own ministers, let him use his discretion and choose them wisely.
Behold the man who can move with the worthy as their intimate: his foes will be powerless against him.
Who can ruin the man that commandeth the friendship of those that can reprove him?
Behold the prince who reposeth not on the support of men who can rebuke him: he will perish even when he hath no foes.
Profit is not for those that have no capital: even so stability is not for them that repose not on the firm support of the wise.
It is foolish to make a multitude of foes: but it is ten times worse to give up the intimacy of the good.
XLVI
Keeping Aloof from Vulgar Company
Men of worth fear vulgar company: but little-minded men mix with it as if they made one family with it.
Water altereth and taketh the character of the soil through which it floweth: even so the mind taketh the colour of the company with which it consorteth.
The understanding of a man belongeth unto his mind: but his reputation dependeth on the company he keepeth.
The disposition of a man seemeth to reside in his mind: but its veritable abode is the company in which he moveth.
Purity of heart and purity of action depend upon the purity of a man’s company.
The pure of heart shall have a righteous progeny: and everything prospereth unto those that consort with good company.
Purity of heart is a treasure unto a man: and virtuous company bringeth him every glory.
Though themselves are endowed with every virtue, the wise looks upon the company of the pure as a tower of strength.
Virtue leadeth unto heaven: and the company of the good steadieth a man in the practice thereof.
There is no greater ally to a man than good company: and nothing injureth so much as evil company.
XLVII
Deliberation Before Action
Take into thy consideration the output and the wastage and the profit that the undertaking will yield: and then put thy hand to it.
Behold the prince who decideth upon action only after consulting with men chosen for their worth: there is nothing that is impossible for him.
There are enterprises that tempt with a great profit but which perish even the capital itself: the wise undertake them not.
Behold the men who fear to be ridiculed by others: they start not on any enterprise without previous deliberation.
To make war without planning every detail of it beforehand is only to transplant thy enemy on carefully prepared soil.
There are things that ought not to be done and if thou do them thou wilt be ruined: and there are things that ought to be done and if thou do them not thou will be ruined also.
Decide not upon any action except after careful deliberation: it is a fool who undertaketh first and sayeth in his heart, I shall think afterwards.
Behold the man that goeth not to his work the right way about: all his labour will be a waste even if numbers come to his aid.
Even in doing good thou mayest err, it thou suit not the benefit to the character of him that receiveth.
Let the thing that thou decidest on be above reproach: for the world despiseth the man who stoopeth to a thing that is beneath himself.
XLVIII
Judging of Strength
Weigh justly the difficulty of the enterprise, thy own strength and the strength of thy enemy, and the strength also of your22 allies; and then enter thou upon it.
Behold the prince who knoweth his own force and hath learned what he ought to learn, and who oversteppeth not the limits his force and information: his invasions will never fail.
Many there have been who in the sanguineness of their hearts overestimated their strength and adventured, but were cut off in the middle.
Behold the men who know not to live in peace, who know not their own measure and who are full of self-conceit: they will have a swift end.
Put too many of them and even peacock’s feathers would break the wagon’s axle.23
Those that have climbed to the top of the tree will lose their lives if they attempt to climb still higher.24
Keep thou in mind the extent of thy wealth and let thy gifts be commensurate therewith: that is the way to conserve and divide thy substance.
It mattereth not if the feeder channel25 is strait, provided that the draining channel26 is not wider.
Behold the man that taketh not account of his measure nor liveth within the bounds thereof: he may look like prospering, but he will perish leaving no trace behind.
Behold the man that measureth not his wealth and lavisheth it with an unsparing hand: his substance will quickly come to nought.
XLIX
Judging the Opportune Moment
The crow triumpheth over the owl when it is day: so opportunity is a great thing to the prince who would vanquish his enemy.
To follow closely on the pace of Time: that is the cord that will bind Fortune to thee firmly.
Where is the thing called impossible if thou start on thy enterprise with a knowledge of the right season and employ the proper means?
Thou canst conquer even the whole world if thou choose the proper time and the proper objectives.
Those that are intent on conquests will be quietly watching their opportunity: they will know neither confusion nor hurry.
The ram steppeth back before it delivereth the crushing blow: even such is the inaction of the man of energy.
The wise show not their anger on the spot: they will nurse it within their hearts and wait for their opportunity.
Bend down before thy adversaries till the day of their decline: when that day is come thou mayest easily throw them down headlong.
When thou hast got an unusual chance, hesitate not but straightway attempt even the impossible.
When the time is against thee feign inaction like the stork: but when the tide is on, strike with the swiftness of its souse.
L
Judging of Place
Provoke no war and begin no operation except after making a thorough reconnaissance of the theatre of operations.
It is an immense advantage even to the powerful and the strong to be based on fortified places.
Even the weak can hold their own and triumph over a powerful foe if they choose the proper theatre and operate cautiously.
The plans of thy adversaries will be baffled if thou fall back on strong positions and base thyself on them.
All-powerful is the crocodile in deep water: but out of it, it is the plaything of its foes.
The strong-wheeled chariot runneth not on the sea: nor saileth the oceangoing ship on dry land.
Behold the prince that hath planned everything beforehand and striketh at the proper objective: he wanteth no other ally than his own valour.
If the prince whose army is weak only betaketh himself to a proper theatre of war, all the endeavours of his strong foe would be vain against him.
Even if they have no proper defences and other advantages it is hard to beat a people on their own soil.
Behold the high-mettled elephant that hath faced without wincing a whole multitude of lancers: even a jackal will triumph over him when he is entangled in marshy ground.
LI
Testing of Men for Confidence
Love of the right, gold, pleasure, and fear of life, these four are the tests of a man: give thy confidence therefore to men that satisfy all these tests.27
Behold the man who is born of a good family, who is free from faults and who dreadeth disgrace: he is the man for thee.
Even men of rare learning and of pure hearts will not be found, when thou dost test them, to be absolutely exempt from all ignorance.
Weigh a man’s good and weigh his evil: whichever is more, take that to be his nature.
Dost thou want to find out whether a man is noble or little-minded? Know that conduct is the touchstone of character.
Beware of trusting men that have no kindred: for their hearts will be without attachment and they will be callous to shame.
If thou choose a fool for thy confidential adviser because that thou lovest him, he will lead thee to endless follies.
Behold the man that trusteth another without trying him: he createth endless evils even unto his posterity.
Trust not a man without trying him: and after trying your men, give each of them the work for which he is fit.
To trust a man whom thou hast not tried and to suspect a man whom thou hast found worthy lead alike to endless ills.
LII
Testing and Employment of Men
Behold the man that seeth the good and seeth the evil also and chooseth only that which is good: employ thou him in thy service.
Behold the man that is able to develop the resources of thy kingdom and to cure the ills that may befall it: set him to manage thy affairs.
Let him alone be selected for service who is endowed with kindness and intelligence and decision, and who is free from greed.
Many are the men that satisfy every test and yet alter in the actual performance of duty.
Work should be entrusted to men in consideration of their expert knowledge and capacity for patient exertion, and not of their love towards thy person.
Choose the expert and give him the work for which he is fit: see that the time is ripe for performance and then get him to begin it.
Determine first the capacity of the servant and the work for which he is fit: and then leave him in responsible charge of the same.
After thou hast decided that a man is fit for an office, make him worthy to fill it.
Behold the man who resenteth the friendly advances of the servant who is skilful at his work: Fortune will depart from him.
Let the prince oversee everything every day: for there will be nothing wrong with the country so long as there is nothing wrong with the officers of the State.
LIII
Cherishing of Kindred
Constancy of attachment even in adversity belongeth only unto kindred.
If a man is blessed with kindred whose love for him bateth not, his fortunes will never cease to grow.
The man who rejoiceth not in the intimacy of his kindred is like a tank without bunds: the waters of prosperity will flow away from him.
To gather and attach one’s kindred to oneself: that is the use and purpose of prosperity.
If a man have a sweet tongue and a liberal hand his kinsmen will gather round him in serried ranks.
Behold the man that giveth freely and entertaineth not anger: the world hath none who hath a more attached kindred than he.
The crow concealeth not its food selfishly from its fellows but shareth it lovingly with them: prosperity will abide only with men of a like nature.
It is good if the prince treateth not all his kinsmen alike but hath a graduated scale for each: for there are many that have an eye to privilege.
The estrangement of a kinsman is easily remedied: remove the cause of the coolness and he will come back to thee.
When a kinsman that hath broken with thee cometh back to thee for a reason, accept thou him, but with caution.
LIV
Guarding Against Insouciance
Worse than excessive rage is the unguardedness that cometh of self-complacency.
A false sense of security killeth glory even as indigence crusheth the understanding.
Glory is not for the unwatchful: that is the conclusion of every school of thinkers in the world.
Of what use are fortresses to the cowardly? or abundance of resources to the incautious?
He who faileth to guard against everything beforehand will deplore his negligence when he is surprised by disaster.
If thou relax not in thy vigilance at all times and against all men, there is nothing like it.
Nothing is impossible to the man who can bring unto his work a mind that is ever wakeful and cautious.
The prince shall devote himself assiduously to works that are commended by the wise: if he neglect them he will suffer in all his future births.
When thou art tempted to be self-complacent and elated, call to thy kind those that have perished by their supineness.
Verily it is easy for a man to achieve all that he desireth, provided he keepeth his purpose constantly before his mind.
LV
Just Government
Deliberate well and lean not to either side: be impartial and consult with the men of law: that is the way to administer justice.
The world looketh up to the rain-cloud for life: even so do men look up to the sceptre of the prince for protection.
The sceptre of the prince is the mainstay of the science of the Brahmans and of righteousness also.
Behold the noble prince who ruleth the people of his dominions with loving care: sovereignty will never depart from him.
Behold the prince who wieldeth the sceptre in accordance with the law: seasonal rains and rich harvests have their home in his land.
It is not the lance that bringeth victory unto the prince: it is rather his sceptre, and that provided it is straight and leaneth not to either side.
The prince is the protector of all his people: and him his sceptre shall guard, provided he alloweth it not ever to lean to either side.
Behold the prince who is not easy of access and who judgeth not causes with care: he will fall from his place and perish, even when he hath no enemy.
Behold the prince that guardeth his subjects from enemies both within and without: if he punish them when they go wrong it is not a blemish: it is his duty.
Punishing the wicked with death is like the removing of weeds from the cornfield.
LVI
Tyranny
Behold the prince who oppresseth his subjects and doth iniquity: he is worse than an assassin.
A request from him who holdeth the sceptre is like the stand and deliver of the highway robber.
Behold the prince who doth not oversee his administration every day and remove the irregularities therein: his sovereignty will wear away day by day.
Behold the thoughtless prince whose rule swerveth from the ways of justice: he will lose his kingdom and his substance also.
Verily it is the tears of those groaning under oppression that wear away the prosperity of the prince.
It is just rule that bringeth renown unto princes: and an unjust government darkeneth their glory.
How fareth the earth under a rainless sky? even so fare the people under the rule of a cruel prince.
The condition of the rich man is more galling than that of the poor under the rule of the tyrant prince.
The heavens will not send showers in their season if the prince swerveth from justice and right.
The udders of the cow will be dried up and the Brahman will forget his science if the prince ruleth not with justice.
LVII
Abstaining from Deeds That Cause Trepidation
The prince shall measure the guilt of the offender and punish him so that he offend not again: but the punishment shall not be excessive.
Those that desire that their power shall last, let them brandish the rod smartly but lay it on soft.
Behold the prince who ruleth with a rod of iron and causeth anguish unto his people: he shall stand without a friend and perish forthwith.
Behold the prince whose cruelty is a byword among his people: his days will be shortened and he will perish forthwith.
Behold the dour-faced prince who is inaccessible to his people: the wealth in his hands is like treasure guarded by a demon.
If the prince is harsh of word and unforgiving, his prosperity, be it ever so great, will come to an end quickly.
Words that are harsh and punishments that are excessive are the files that file away the iron of power.
Behold the prince who will not take counsel with his councillors but who falleth into a passion when his projects fail: his prosperity will wane away.
Behold the prince who looketh not to his defences while yet there is time: when he is surprised by a war be will be seized with trembling and perish quickly.
The tyranny that yoketh to itself charlatans is the only burden under which the earth groaneth: there is none other beside.
LVIII
Considerateness
Behold that ravishing Beauty called Considerateness: the world cannot go on smoothly without her.
In considerateness have the amenities of life their existence: those who possess it not are a burden unto the earth.
To what end is the song that cannot be sung? and what is the worth of the eye that showeth not indulgence?
What is the use of eyes that merely show in the face, if they show not consideration for others according to their measure?
Indulgence is the ornament of the eye: the eye that hath it not will be looked upon as a mere sore.
Behold the men whose eyes show not consideration towards others: verily they are no better than the trees of the earth.
Verily they are blind, those who are not considerate towards others: and there are none that truly see but are indulgent to others’ faults.
Behold the man who can be considerate towards others without derogating from any of his duties: he will inherit the earth.
It is nobility to forbear and show indulgence even unto those that have offended thee.
Those who desire to be styled the very pink of courtesy will drink off even the poison that hath been mixed for them before their very eyes.
LIX
The Service of Intelligence
Let the prince understand that Political Science and his Intelligence Corps are the eyes wherewith he seeth.
It is the duty of the prince to learn betimes everything that befalleth every man and every day.
Behold the prince that learneth not the happenings about him by means of scouts and spies: conquests are not for him.
The prince shalt set spies to watch closely the officers of the realm, his own kindred, and his enemies.

Behold the man who can wear an unsuspicious appearance, who will not know confusion before any man, and who can guard his secrets from ever leaking out: he is the proper man for the work of Intelligence.
Spies and scouts shall disguise themselves as ascetics and holy men, and their investigation shall be thorough: and whatever is done them, they shall not let out their secrets.
Behold the man who can draw out secrets from others and whose information is ever unconfused and clear: he is the man for the work of intelligence.
Even the information that hath been obtained by a spy shall be tested by that of another.
See that no spy knoweth the others engaged in the same work: when three reports agree, thou mayest give credence to them.
Reward not openly thy officers of Intelligence: for if thou do, thou merely lettest out thy own secret.
LX
Energy
Those that possess energy are alone to be called rich: as to those that possess it not, do they really possess what they own?
Energy is the veritable possession of a man: for wealth endureth not forever and will depart from him one day.
Behold the men that hold in their hands the resource called energy: they will never despair, saying, Alas, we are ruined!
Behold the man who remitteth not ever from his activity: Good Fortune inquireth the way to his home.
The water with which a plant is watered is the measure of the luxuriance of its flower: even so, the spirit of a man is the measure of his fortunes.
Let all thy purposes be grand: for then even if they fail, their glory will tarnish never.
Men of spirit flinch not before a defeat: the elephant planteth his legs only more firmly when he is hit by the deep-piercing arrow.
Behold the men that are wanting in energy: the glory of an exhaustless liberality can never be theirs.
What availeth his size and his sharp tapering tusks? The heart of the elephant sinketh when he seeth the tiger spring.
Exuberance of spirit, that alone is strength: those that have it not are mere stocks: their human bodies alone make the difference.
LXI
Abstention from Sloth
The perennial light called Family will be extinguished if it is invaded by the foul vapour of sloth.
Let them call sloth by its real name and avoid it, those who desire to establish their family on a solid foundation.
Behold the fool who huggeth assassin sloth unto his heart: his family will fall even before his day is ended.
Behold the men who are sunk in sloth and who turn not their hand to any noble undertakings: their family will go to ruin and their vices will grow apace.
Procrastination, forgetfulness, sloth, and sleep, these four are the cosy pleasure boats of those that are fated to perish.
The slothful can never thrive in the world even though they have the favour of princes.
Behold the men who are slothful and who turn not their hand to any noble undertakings: they will listen to much reproof and contumely.
If sloth find a home in a family, the family will soon be in bondage to its foes.
The afflictions that may have befallen a man’s family will cease to exist the moment he giveth up sloth.
Behold the prince that knoweth not sloth: he will bring within his sway all that hath been measured by the steps of Trivikrama.28
LXII
Manly Exertion
Shrink not from any work saying, It is impossible: for labour will give thee the strength to achieve everything.
Beware of leaving any work unfinished: for the world careth not for those that do not complete the work that they have once begun.
The proud pleasure of being able to serve all men belongeth only to the greatness that shrinketh not from any exertion.
Like unto a sword in the hands of a eunuch is the liberality of the indolent man: it will not endure.
The man who loveth not pleasure but loveth work is a pillar of strength unto his friends and will wipe away their tears of grief.
Industry is the mother of Prosperity: but Indolence only bringeth forth Misery.
In sloth hath the Genius of Wretchedness her home: but the Lotus-born One29 resideth in the labour of him who yieldeth not to sloth.
It is no shame if fortune faileth a man but it is a disgrace if he abstain deliberately from exertion.
Even though the Gods be against, Industry is bound to pay the wages of labour.
They will snap their fingers even at Destiny who succumb not to it but labour unremittingly in despite of it.
LXIII
Intrepidity in the Face of Misfortune
When thou meetest with misfortune face it with thy best smile: for there is nothing like a smile to enable a man to hold his own against it.
A whole sea of troubles will abase themselves the moment a shifty mind collecteth itself to face them.
Troubles they send away troubled who trouble not themselves at the sight of troubles.
Behold the man who is prepared to strain his every nerve like the bull-buffalo to wade through every difficulty: he may meet with obstacles but he will send them away disappointed.
Behold the man whose heart sinketh not even at a whole host of troubles arrayed against him: the obstacles in his path have themselves met with an obstacle.
The men that exult not at good fortune, can they ever fret themselves saying, Alas! we are ruined?
The wise know that the body is a target unto misfortune: and so they worry themselves not when they meet with a calamity.
Behold the man who loveth not pleasure and who knoweth that difficulties are a part of the law of things: he smarteth not ever under any check.
The man who runneth not after pleasure in the day of success suffereth not pain in the day of failure.
Behold the man who looketh upon the stress and strain of exertion as a veritable joy: he will be extolled by his very enemies.
Section II
The Members of the Body Politic
LXIV
The Councillor of State
Behold the man who judgeth aright the ways and means of achieving great enterprises and the proper season to commence them: he is the proper man for the Council.
Study, resolution, manly exertion, and loving attention to the welfare of the people, these four make along with the last the five qualifications of the Councillor.
He is the able minister who possesseth the capacity to disunite allies, to cherish and keep up existing friendships, and to reunite those who have become enemies.
Judgment in the choice of projects and the means of their execution, and positiveness in the expression of opinion are necessary qualities in the Councillor.
Behold the man who knoweth the law and aboundeth in instruction, is deliberate in his speech and always understandeth what is fit for each occasion: he is the Councillor for thee.
What is there that is too subtle for men who add knowledge of books unto natural intelligence?
Even though thou art wise in thy knowledge of books, gather thou the wisdom of experience and act in accordance therewith.
The prince may be a fool and may thwart him at every step: but the duty of the Councillor is always to point to him what is just and proper.
Behold the minister that sitteth in the Council and plotteth the ruin of his prince: he is more dangerous than seven hundred million enemies.
The irresolute may even plan perfectly: but they will waver in the course of the execution and will never accomplish their designs.
LXV
Eloquence
The blessing of the tongue is a blessing indeed: for it is a blessing apart and formeth not part of other blessings.
Death and life are in the power of the tongue: guard thou therefore against imprudence of speech.
Behold the speech that bindeth friends more closely and fascinateth even enemies: that alone is worthy of its name.
Weigh each circumstance aright and then speak the speech that is fit: for the increase of righteousness and profit there is no other thing of more worth to thee than it.
Speak thou the speech that cannot be silenced by any other speech.
To speak so as to captivate one’s own hearers and to seize the sense in the words of others, that is the part of the consummate statesman.
Behold the man who is eloquent of speech and knoweth neither confusion nor fear: it is impossible for anyone to beat him in debate.
Behold the men whose speech is well ordered and couched in persuasive language: the world will be at their beck and call.
Verily they have a passion for much speaking who know not to say their mind in few and well chosen words.
Behold the men who cannot expound unto others the knowledge that they have acquired: they are like unto the flower that blossometh but giveth forth no fragrance.
LXVI
Purity of Action
Alliances bring success unto a man: but purity of action fulfilleth his every desire.
Always turn thy face away from those deeds that bring not glory as well as profit.
Those that desire to rise in the world, let them abjure all action that can tarnish their glory.
Behold the men who see things in their right proportions: even when fallen on evil days they stoop not to action that is dishonourable and mean.
Let not a man do those things which make him cry afterwards, what is it that I have done? and if he hath done any such thing, it is good for him if he doth it not once again.
Let not a man do those things that good men condemn, even to save the mother that bore him from starvation.
The indigence of the worthy is better far than wealth that is amassed by dishonourable means.
Behold the men that shun not those things that are forbidden by good morals: they will come to grief even if they succeed in their designs.
All that is wrong in the midst of tears will depart also accompanied by weepings: but that which is acquired by righteous ways, even if lost in the middle, increaseth in the latter end.
To try to lay by wealth by means of guile is like trying to preserve water in a pot of clay that is not baked.
LXVII
Decision of Character
Greatness of achievement is nought else but the greatness of the will that striveth therefor: all other things come not near the mark.
To avoid all action that is bound to fail and not to turn away from one’s purpose because of obstacles: these two are said to be the guiding principles of the wise.
The man of action letteth his purpose appear only when that purpose is achieved: for an untimely disclosure would create obstacles that cannot be surmounted.
To say a thing is easy for any man: but to do it in the manner undertaken is a rare thing indeed.
Behold the man who hath acquired a name for the doing of great deeds: his services will be greatly in request with the prince and will be esteemed by all.
That which they will, men acquire even in the manner that they will, provided they will with all their might.
Despise not a man for his look: for there are men who are even as the axle pin of the mighty rolling car.
When thou hast resolved upon a thing with all thy wits about thee, waver not but pursue thy purpose with vigour.
Take up the doing of works that increase happiness: and even if thou have to suffer cruel mortification in the doing of them, steel thy heart and persevere to the end.
Behold the men that have not the ambition to do great deeds: the world will not care for them whatever their other virtues may be.
LXVIII
The Conduct of Affairs
The end of all deliberation is to arrive at a decision: and when a decision is come to, it is wrong to delay the execution thereof.
Do with deliberation those things that ought to be done in a leisurely way: but put not off even for a moment those things that require prompt action.
Go straight for the goal whenever circumstances permit: but when circumstances are against, follow along the path that offereth the least resistance.
Uncompleted work and enemies that are left unsubdued are like unextinguished sparks of fire: they will grow betimes and overwhelm the perfunctory man.

Five things should be carefully considered in the doing of all action, namely, the resources in band, the instrument, the nature of the action itself, the proper time and the proper place for its execution.
Determine first the exertion necessary, the obstacles in the way, and the expected profit, and then undertake thy enterprise.
The way to succeed in any undertaking is to learn the secret thereof from the man who is an expert in it.
Men decoy one elephant by means of another: even so make one enterprise the means of achieving a second.
Placate enemies even more swiftly than thou rewardest friends.
The weak should not care to live in the midst of constant alarms: when an opportunity offereth itself they should submit to an alliance with the strong.
LXIX
The Ambassador
